issue.issue_text: Challenge to the conviction and sentence for the offence of homicide, not amounting to murder.

facts: The appellants and the victim were cousins with a pre-existing dispute.
The appellants, armed with an axe, attacked the victim, striking him on the head, which is a vital part of the body.
The victim died 20 days after the attack.
The post-mortem report, supported by the doctor's testimony (PW14), concluded that death was caused by cardio-respiratory failure as a direct result of the injuries inflicted by the appellants.

The appellants argued that the conviction should be for culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Sec 304 IPC) due to 'grave and sudden provocation' and because the 20-day time lapse showed the injuries were not sufficient to cause death.
law: The central legal issue is the distinction between murder (Section 302 IPC) and the lesser offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304 IPC).
An exception to murder can be 'grave and sudden provocation' (under Section 300 IPC), but the burden to prove the existence of such provocation lies with the accused.
The lapse of time between the infliction of an injury and the victim's death is not, by itself (per se), a determinative factor that reduces an offender's liability from murder to culpable homicide.
The critical test is the nature of the injury and whether it was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, thereby establishing a direct causal link between the act and the death.
application: The Court rejected the 'grave and sudden provocation' argument, stating there was no evidence that the pre-existing dispute had been aggravated or that the victim did anything to trigger a loss of self-control in the appellants. The appellants failed to provide any evidence to support this claim.

The Court dismissed the significance of the 20-day delay in the victim's death, citing several precedents where murder convictions were upheld even when death occurred 12 to 15 days after the attack. It held there is no 'stereotypical formula' regarding time lapse.
The Court found a direct and close link between the injuries and the death, relying on the medical evidence which established that the death was a result of the injuries inflicted by the appellants.
The Court noted that the appellants came armed with an axe and attacked a vital part of the body (the head), which demonstrated pre-meditation and an intent consistent with murder.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no infirmity in the High Court's judgment. It concluded that the prosecution had proven the elements of murder and that the appellants' arguments for reducing the charge were without merit. Consequently, the Court rejected the challenge, upheld the conviction and sentence for murder, and dismissed the appeal.

respondent_arguments: The concurrent findings of the lower courts do not contain any glaring infirmity or error and do not warrant interference.
The credibility of eyewitness PW1 cannot be questioned, as she was also a victim of the attack.
The evidence of PW1 was corroborated on all material aspects by other witnesses (PW2, PW3, and PW4).
The depositions by the two doctors support the conviction.
The victim never recovered from his injuries, was unable to record a statement, and died in the hospital 20 days after the incident, establishing a direct link between the assault and death.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellants failed to establish that their actions fell under the exception of 'grave and sudden' provocation. A long-standing, pre-existing dispute does not, by itself, constitute a 'sudden' provocation, and the appellants provided no evidence of a specific, immediate trigger that would cause a reasonable person to lose self-control. Therefore, their attempt to reduce the charge from murder to culpable homicide under Exception 1 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code was rejected.
legal_tests_applied: The test for 'grave and sudden' provocation is whether a reasonable man, belonging to the same class of society as the accused and placed in the same situation, would be so provoked as to lose his self-control. (K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra)

The standard for an act being so imminently dangerous as to cause death (Section 300 fourthly) emphasizes the accused’s disregard for the consequences of the injury and an element of callousness to the result, which signifies intention.

To bring a case under Section 300 '3rdly', the prosecution must prove: First, that a bodily injury is present; second, the nature of the injury; third, that there was an intention to inflict that particular injury (not accidental or unintentional); and fourth, that the injury was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature. (Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab)
why_appellant_lost: The appellants failed to show what caused the “sudden” provocation, relying only on a pre-existing dispute, which was insufficient to meet the legal standard.
The appellants did not lead any evidence to substantiate their claim of acting under grave and sudden provocation, which is necessary to fall within Exception 1 to Section 300.
The evidence on record did not support the contention that the appellants' actions were the result of a loss of self-control arising from a grave and sudden provocation.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that a pre-existing dispute could not be considered a 'grave and sudden' provocation.
The respondent established that the victim's survival for a period of time after the attack was irrelevant, as the cause of death was directly linked to the injuries inflicted by the appellants.
policy_considerations: The standard of a 'reasonable man' for the purpose of 'grave and sudden' provocation is not an abstract concept; it must be contextualized based on the customs, manners, way of life, and the cultural, social, and emotional background of the society to which the accused belongs.

It is neither possible nor desirable to lay down a precise, universal standard for what constitutes 'grave and sudden' provocation; it is for the court to decide in each case, having regard to the relevant circumstances.
